sourceFamilies: regulator (FDA GRAS notice, FDA structure/function-claims policy)
professional position stand / systematic review (ISSN 2017; BMC Nephrology 2025 meta-analysis)
research.headline: Creatine monohydrate has strong, well-replicated human evidence for high-intensity/resistance-exercise performance and is GRAS as a food ingredient (not an FDA-approved drug), with a 2025 kidney-function meta-analysis and a 2025 RCT directly rebutting the popular hair-loss/DHT claim, while renal safety in people with pre-existing kidney impairment remains comparatively under-studied.

sourceFamilies: controlled-human-study (VITAL trial, COVID RCT via secondary summaries)
research.headline: The largest RCT of high-dose vitamin D3 (VITAL, NEJM 2019) and USPSTF's own guideline both found no benefit for the primary-prevention uses (cancer, cardiovascular disease, fractures, falls) most associated with the compound, while popular online marketing for immune support, mood, and COVID protection outpaces the weak-to-negative controlled evidence for those specific claims.

issues: Warning (style/drift): claim creatine-safety-common-adverse-effects-001 opens with 'Creatine is considered safe for short-term use by healthy adults' — a near-verbatim paraphrase of the NIH source's own bare 'safe' language. It is population/duration-qualified (short-term, healthy adults) and directly sourced, so it is not a blocker, but it sits close to the safety-assurance pattern the audit is watching for; the follow-on ISSN quote ('safe and well-tolerated ... up to 30 g/day for 5 years') is properly dose/duration-scoped. Recommend tightening to attribute the 'safe' language explicitly to the cited source in-line (e.g. 'NIH's fact sheet states creatine is considered safe...') to remove any ambiguity that this is the packet's own assurance.

Warning (style/drift): claim vitamind3-adverse-effect-hypercalcemia-toxicity-001 embeds the product label's imperative text verbatim ('Do not exceed recommended dosage. Consult your physician before taking this product if you have vascular disease...'). This is a faithful quote of the source's required warning language (not the packet's own invented advice) and is explicitly framed as 'safety context, not a treatment protocol,' so not a blocker — but because it reads as second-person medical instruction, reviewers should confirm at sign-off that no downstream consumer-facing surface renders this claim's statement text as if it were BioStack's own advice rather than a quoted label warning.

Already self-flagged by the packet (not a new finding, confirmed correct): the VITAL-trial efficacy claim rests on a secondary media summary (TCTMD) because the primary NEJM/PMC text was inaccessible this session. Spot-checked TCTMD directly — both quotes used in the packet were located verbatim in the live article — so the claim is currently well-supported by the source actually cited, but the packet's own reviewReasons correctly keep it human-review-gated pending primary-source reconciliation.

warnings: creatine.evidence.json: 'considered safe for short-term use by healthy adults' phrasing in creatine-safety-common-adverse-effects-001 borders on unqualified safety assurance despite having population/duration context; consider more explicit source-attribution framing.

vitamin-d3.evidence.json: hypercalcemia claim quotes label imperative/second-person warning text verbatim; correctly disclaimed as label content, but worth a style pass so it cannot be mistaken for original medical advice.
